classification.difficultyReason: Combine binomial expansion and triangle areas to establish Pythagoras’ theorem geometrically.

content.prompt: In Chapter 8 we gave a proof of Pythagoras’ theorem that relied on rearranging triangles and comparing areas in two diagrams. We now give a proof using just one diagram.

spec.sourceRegion: Upper-right diagram beside Pythagoras’ theorem parts a–c
spec.description: An enclosing square contains a tilted white square and four corner right triangles. Light blue distinguishes the four triangle regions used together in the area subtraction; ordinary edges and labels use black.
spec.mathematics: Each corner triangle has perpendicular legs a and b and hypotenuse c. The outer square has side a+b. Clockwise inner vertices lie on the top near the right, right near the bottom, bottom near the left and left near the top. All four inner sides are labelled c.
spec.answerVisibility: All source labels and regions are permanent givens. No computed areas or proof steps appear in the question diagram.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the total area of the four triangles is $2ab$.

answer.short: Each triangle has area $\frac12ab$, so the total area is $4\times\frac12ab=2ab$.
answer.worked:
Each right-angled triangle has perpendicular base and height $a$ and $b$, so its area is $\frac12ab$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Total triangle area}&=4\times\frac12ab\\\text{Total triangle area}&=2ab\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$c^2=(a+b)^2-2ab=a^2+b^2$.

Subtract the four triangles’ total area from the enclosing square’s area.
answer.worked:
The inner square has area $c^2$. Its area plus the four triangles’ area equals the enclosing square’s area.
$$\begin{align*}c^2+2ab&=(a+b)^2\\c^2+2ab&=a^2+2ab+b^2\\c^2&=a^2+2ab+b^2-2ab\\c^2&=a^2+b^2\end{align*}$$
